newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's 1997 budget seen setting conservative tone.
newsitem.headline: Peru's 1997 budget seen setting conservative tone.

text.p: Peru's 1997 budget proposal sets a conservative macroeconomic framework with a tight fiscal line and a clear commitment to pay foreign debt, analysts said.
The government's budget plans also leave ample space for tackling Peru's deep-rooted social problems, but makes this area susceptible to political influence, they added.

"It's a very conservative budget," said Oscar Jasaui, head of the Lima Economists Association. "It shows an intention to maintain a fiscal balance, and a willingness to make good on debt, while also maintaining a large social component, although unfortunately this component is subject to political factors."

President Alberto Fujimori's government recently sent Congress, for approval by November 30, its proposal for a 24.765 billion sol budget in 1997 -- nominally higher than this year's 22.263 billion soles but, lower in real terms factoring in 1996 inflation of about 12 percent.
The pro-Fujimori Congress is expected to approve the government's proposal with little opposition.
The budget commits 18.7 percent of funds next year to debt payment, up from 14.1 percent this year, and 44 percent to social spending, up from 40 percent in 1996.

Key macroeconomic forecasts for next year include economic growth of five percent, inflation of nine percent, an average exchange rate of 2.70 soles to the dollar (from 2.49 now), and a $1.6 billion trade deficit.
While the Economy Ministry has the largest share of the budget, 26.4 percent, this includes debt payments, meaning the real winner is the increasingly powerful Presidency Ministry.
This ministry has 22.6 percent of the budget and oversees social spending, often at the discretion of the president.

"Having such a large lump of money under the presidency makes it subject to political motives," said another local analyst, who asked not to be named. "If not used wisely, it could upset the otherwise measured fiscal policy."

Carlos Blanco Oropeza, president of Congress' budget committee, said the 1997 budget was designed within the tight framework of the government's three-year macroeconomic target with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
"If there is no income, there is no spending ... nor are we going to start printing money at the central bank," he said.

Blanco added that the increase in funds for debt payment were intended to cover an estimated extra $100 million for Paris Club creditors and between $230 million and $250 million for the commercial banks after the completion of a Brady deal.

"It looks like a very tight budget," said a Peru analyst on Wall Street. "You have low expenses and a very conservative monetary policy. It's very focused, very specific. You have to give them credit for that."
While the budget may have Peru's foreign followers happy, there has not been unanimous support at home.

Critics and opposition legislators say the 44 percent figure for social spending disguises massive bureaucratic costs, and they claim that in reality the budget sacrifices domestic needs for increased foreign debt service.
"It produces a bigger transfer abroad of resources that could reactivate our economic activity so as to pay debt afterwards to the rich countries," said opposition deputy Manuel Lazo.

"Having reduced the budget in real terms and having increased the participation of debt service, there are no better prospects for the necessary increases in salaries of specific groups of public workers -- education, health, etc."
Most polls show unemployment, poverty and salary levels to be Peruvians' main current concerns.
Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi, however, insisted during a recent presentation to Congress that such needs were paramount in the budget.

"The fundamental objective ... is the raising of the standard of living of all Peruvians, particularly the poorest. This is to be achieved through consolidation of macroeconomic stabilization, recovery of growth, generation of employment and sustained support to the social program," he said.
Pandolfi said the government had already brought extreme poverty down to 19 percent this year from 22 percent in 1991, and hoped to reduce it further to 11 percent in 2000.
-- Lima newsroom, 511 221-2134
